notes.subject: plate
notes.text: Long white plates with a blue strip on the left and, on most, a yellow strip on the right, unique here. The yellow strip ended in 2020.

notes.subject: pole
notes.text: Concrete ladder poles with very tall steps, each often with a small see-through hole. In Spain and France the steps are short.

notes.subject: sign
notes.text: Chevrons are black with yellow arrows, the only Mediterranean country with this scheme.

notes.subject: sign
notes.text: Red and white hunting signs, diamond or rectangular, are common in rural areas. Spanish ones are white and black.

notes.subject: landscape
notes.text: Eucalyptus trees are very common; the only other part of Europe where they are is northern Spain.

notes.subject: bollard
notes.text: Either wedge bollards with a thin white top, or flat ones with a wide reflector; reflectors are mostly white, sometimes orange, darker than Spain's yellow.

notes.subject: guardrail
notes.text: A-type guardrails with red reflectors; Spain uses yellow.

notes.subject: sign
notes.text: Direction signs are mostly white with black arrows that do not touch the border. Spain uses colourful road number boxes.

notes.subject: sign
notes.text: Road signs are typically encased by a white border; most Spanish ones have none.

notes.subject: sign
notes.text: Stop signs have a fairly large font, whereas Spain's text is small and compact.

notes.subject: sign
notes.text: Pedestrian sign has five stripes and a figure with a noticeably high belt. Spain has eight stripes; Italy's figure has no belt.

notes.subject: sign
notes.text: Wide rectangular kilometre markers with a diagonally divided coloured section on the left; black and white waystones are common too.

notes.subject: language
notes.text: A Romance language like Spanish, but with Ç Ã Õ Â Ê and no Ñ. The word for road is "Rua"; the northwest neighbour writes "Rúa".

notes.subject: other
notes.text: Cobblestone roads with square stones laid diagonally to the road, and sidewalks of distinctly bright cobbles, are very common.

notes.subject: architecture
notes.text: White painted stone houses with orange tiled roofs, often trimmed with blue or yellow lines around windows, doors and walls.

notes.subject: architecture
notes.text: Houses covered in decorative mosaic tiles are somewhat common.

notes.subject: architecture
notes.text: Decorative round or square chimneys with small spire tops are very common in the south; round ones are a strong clue.

notes.subject: architecture
notes.text: Houses of square concrete blocks joined with white mortar in the north; the northwest neighbour has them without white mortar.

notes.subject: landscape
notes.text: Sparse open fields of small holm and cork oaks in the southeast, dry in summer and lush in spring.

notes.subject: landscape
notes.text: Olive plantations in dense rows, mostly in the eastern half; oaks are planted more sparsely with no pattern.

notes.subject: landscape
notes.text: Dense eucalyptus forests are mostly in the northwest; maritime pine plantations, with grey bark and upward fluffy branches, are common in the northern half.

notes.subject: landscape
notes.text: Steep terraced vineyards in the wine valley due east of Porto.

notes.subject: landscape
notes.text: Citrus plantations mostly along the south coast.

notes.subject: landscape
notes.text: Rocky mountain highland with yellow and black striped snow poles in the central natural park.

notes.subject: landscape
notes.text: Pine forests on very sandy white soil near the coast between Setúbal and Sines.

notes.subject: landscape
notes.text: Flat, dry, uncultivated land in the far southwest with only low bushes and grass.

notes.subject: sign
notes.text: Lime green street signs are found in Porto.
